\section{Conclusion}

We present the first causal, type-granularity study of how policy ambiguity causes safety violations in LLM agents. Across 2,997 episodes with five architecturally diverse models, ambiguous policy clauses increase violation rates by 34.0 pp. The effect is universal but not uniform: a three-tier type hierarchy and a model$\times$type interaction reveal that safety training differentially mitigates specific ambiguity types, with authorization scope as a ``canary type'' and incompleteness as a universal blind spot. Fewer than 11\% of ambiguous episodes show any disambiguation awareness, establishing Ambiguity Blindness as an empirical phenomenon. These findings motivate type-aware policy auditing pipelines and externalized ambiguity detection as complementary defenses for deployed agent systems.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\paragraph{Model coverage.} We evaluate five API-accessible models (three proprietary, two open-source). Smaller open-source models (7B--70B parameters) may show different vulnerability patterns, and our findings may not generalize to models with fundamentally different training approaches.

\paragraph{Domain scope.} $\tau^2$-bench covers retail and airline customer service. Policy ambiguity effects in other domains (healthcare, finance, legal) remain to be tested, though the within-study cross-domain consistency (airline vs.\ retail $\Delta < 13$ pp) is encouraging.

\paragraph{Synthetic ambiguity.} Our matched-pair design requires synthetic construction of ambiguous variants, which may not capture the full distribution of naturally occurring policy ambiguities. We mitigate this through expert review of all clause pairs and design constraints requiring naturalistic formulations.

\paragraph{Cross-judge asymmetry.} Our evaluation uses GPT-4.1 to judge GPT-5.4 traces and GPT-5.4 to judge all other models. A mid-tier model judging a frontier model may miss subtle violations that a stronger judge would catch, potentially underestimating GPT-5.4's true violation rate.

\paragraph{Failure mode analysis.} The qualitative coding of 245 violation traces covers only GPT-5.4 and GPT-4.1. Extending this analysis to all five models would strengthen the generalizability of the failure mode taxonomy. Automated inter-coder agreement (Gwet's AC1 $= 0.78$) provides moderate validation, but human annotation of a subset would further increase confidence.

\paragraph{Incompleteness confound.} Incompleteness clause pairs involve adding information to the unambiguous variant, creating an information asymmetry beyond pure disambiguation. We address this through dual-track analysis (within-type and cross-type comparisons) and note it as a caveat for incompleteness-specific effect size estimates.

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	A customer asks to return a customized item within the 30-day window. The agent consults the store policy, which states that ``items may be returned within 30 days.'' The word ``items'' scopes over all product categories, including custom orders that are normally final sale. The agent grants a full refund and arranges free return shipping. One word of scopal ambiguity costs the retailer \$200.
5	
6	LLM-based agents increasingly operate under natural-language policy specifications that govern their permitted actions. These specifications inevitably contain ambiguity: a property that has been studied for decades in requirements engineering (RE) and computational linguistics. \citet{berry_kamsties_2004} distinguish between \emph{nocuous} ambiguity, where different stakeholders arrive at different interpretations, and \emph{innocuous} ambiguity, where shared organizational context ensures convergent interpretation. In human RE workflows, most ambiguity is innocuous because developers share domain knowledge, can consult colleagues, and iteratively clarify requirements.
7	
8	LLM agents lack these disambiguation channels. They cannot consult colleagues, rarely escalate to users, and must resolve ambiguity in real time from the text alone. This raises a question that has not been empirically addressed: does policy ambiguity cause safety violations in LLM agents, and if so, does the \emph{type} of ambiguity predict the severity of the violation? 1	\section*{Limitations}
2	\label{sec:limitations}
3	
4	\paragraph{Model coverage.} We evaluate five API-accessible models (three proprietary, two open-source). Smaller open-source models (7B--70B parameters) may show different vulnerability patterns, and our findings may not generalize to models with fundamentally different training approaches.
5	
6	\paragraph{Domain scope.} $\tau^2$-bench covers retail and airline customer service. Policy ambiguity effects in other domains (healthcare, finance, legal) remain to be tested, though the within-study cross-domain consistency (airline vs.\ retail $\Delta < 13$ pp) is encouraging.
7	
8	\paragraph{Synthetic ambiguity.} Our matched-pair design requires synthetic construction of ambiguous variants, which may not capture the full distribution of naturally occurring policy ambiguities. We mitigate this through expert review of all clause pairs and design constraints requiring naturalistic formulations.
9	
10	\paragraph{Cross-judge asymmetry.} Our evaluation uses GPT-4.1 to judge GPT-5.4 traces and GPT-5.4 to judge all other models. A mid-tier model judging a frontier model may miss subtle violations that a stronger judge would catch, potentially underestimating GPT-5.4's true violation rate.
11	
12	\paragraph{Failure mode analysis.} The qualitative coding of 245 violation traces covers only GPT-5.4 and GPT-4.1. Extending this analysis to all five models would strengthen the generalizability of the failure mode taxonomy. Automated inter-coder agreement (Gwet's AC1 $= 0.78$) provides moderate validation, but human annotation of a subset would further increase confidence.
13	
14	\paragraph{Incompleteness confound.} Incompleteness clause pairs involve adding information to the unambiguous variant, creating an information asymmetry beyond pure disambiguation. We address this through dual-track analysis (within-type and cross-type comparisons) and note it as a caveat for incompleteness-specific effect size estimates.
